title: The House of Visible Speech: the Telephone, the Deaf, and the Mountain at Baddeck
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Edinburgh, the birth on South Charlotte Street
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected from the gathering pass's 55.9497, -3.2071, which fell 130 to 180 m southwest of the street; Nominatim places South Charlotte Street EH2 at 55.9505 to 55.9511 N.
stops.campa: At 16 South Charlotte Street a third son is born to Alexander Melville Bell, teacher of elocution, and Eliza Grace Symonds, miniature painter and pianist, who is losing her hearing in middle life. The father is building a written alphabet of the human mouth, a set of symbols for every position the tongue and the lips can take, and he calls it Visible Speech. The mother follows conversation by watching faces and by a rubber tube pressed against her forehead. The house holds both facts at once: a notation for every sound a person can make, and a woman who cannot hear one of them.
suggested_refs: The stone inscription on 16 South Charlotte Street, Edinburgh, marking the birthplace

stops.name: Royal High School, Edinburgh, the mill and the middle name
stops.date_confidence: attested for the events, approximate for the day. The middle name is taken c. 1858 at age ten or eleven; the dehusking machine is dated 1859; he leaves the Royal High School in 1862. Three years compressed into one pin.
stops.campa: He asks his father for a middle name, wanting what his two brothers have, and takes Graham from a Canadian boarder the family is fond of. At twelve he builds a dehusking machine of rotating paddles and stiff brushes for a neighbour's flour mill, and it works. At the Royal High School he completes four of the six forms and leaves, an indifferent scholar with no prizes. At home he is already working the family dog's jaw with his hands while it growls on command, making it produce a few blurred syllables for visitors, and calling the result a talking dog.
suggested_refs: The Royal High School building on Calton Hill, Edinburgh
sources: The talking-dog episode is biographical tradition, not present in the sources fetched for this pass

stops.name: Harrington Square, London, the year with the grandfather
stops.date_confidence: attested, and corrected. The gathering pass gave c.1862-1865; Wikipedia says 'During the year he spent with his grandfather', and Bell is at Elgin by 1863, so the stay is a single year.
stops.campa: Out of school at fifteen, he goes south to London to live with his grandfather, another Alexander Bell, in the terrace on Harrington Square by Mornington Crescent. The old man is an elocutionist too. He dresses the boy in a gentleman's clothes and sets him to reading aloud from the classics for hours at a stretch. Bell arrives a Scottish schoolboy with four forms of Latin behind him, and leaves a year later able to hold a room. Then he goes north again, to be paid for it.
suggested_refs: The Harrington Square terrace near Mornington Crescent, London

stops.name: Weston House Academy, Elgin, the pupil-teacher
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year. Exact building within Elgin unconfirmed by any source fetched; the pin is the town.
stops.campa: At sixteen he is hired at Weston House Academy in Elgin as a pupil-teacher of elocution and music, taking Greek and Latin as a student in the same building where he teaches boys barely younger than himself. It is his first paid work and his first classroom. What he teaches here he will go on teaching for sixty years: the training of the voice by way of the physiology of the mouth, on his father's conviction that speech is a mechanism. A mechanism can be taught to anybody who has the parts for it.
suggested_refs: Weston House Academy, Elgin, Moray, site of his first teaching post

stops.name: Somerset College, Bath, the first brother buried
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of both the post and the death. Exact address in Bath unconfirmed; the pin is the city centre.
stops.campa: He teaches at Somerset College in Bath, one post in a run of English schoolmastering that fills the years between Elgin and the emigration. In this year his younger brother Edward dies of tuberculosis. Bell is twenty. The family begins the arithmetic every consumptive household in Britain performs: which climate, which coast, how soon, and whether the thing is already in the survivors. He goes on teaching, and in the following year passes the matriculation examinations at Edinburgh and is accepted at University College London.
suggested_refs: Somerset College, Bath, one of the English posts of 1867-1868

stops.name: South Kensington, the school of Susanna Hull
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1868-1870. Exact street address unconfirmed. His attendance at University College London in the same period is tagged reconstruction in the research pool, resting on Robert V. Bruce's 1973 biography.
stops.campa: At Susanna Hull's private school in South Kensington he teaches deaf children directly for the first time, applying his father's symbols to pupils who have never heard the sounds the symbols describe. He is attending lectures at University College London in the same months. In May 1870 his elder brother Melville dies of the same disease that took Edward, leaving Alexander the only surviving son of three, and the father, who has now buried two, sells the London practice inside the summer and books passage for Canada.
suggested_refs: Susanna E. Hull's private school for deaf children, South Kensington, London
sources: Robert V. Bruce, 'Bell: Alexander Graham Bell and the Conquest of Solitude' (1973), for the UCL attendance, not re-verified

segments.name: Tutelo Heights and the Boston Schools

stops.name: Paris, Ontario, the minister's house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month inferred from the family's summer arrival and the purchase of the Brantford farm before winter.
stops.campa: The family lands in Canada and Alexander lodges first with the Baptist minister Thomas Henderson in Paris, Ontario, a mill town on the Grand River. He is twenty-three, and by the reckoning of everyone who looks at him he is dying: the same cough, the same house, the same odds that killed Melville in May and Edward three years before. The climate is the whole prescription. Within months the cough is gone. His father buys a farm eight miles downriver and the household moves onto it before the winter closes the roads.
suggested_refs: The Henderson house at Paris, Ontario, first Canadian lodging

stops.name: Melville House, Tutelo Heights, the dreaming place
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected from the gathering pass's 43.1233, -80.2453, wrong by about 2.7 km; Wikipedia gives 43.10750, -80.270417 for 94 Tutela Heights Road. Acreage is given as 10.5 in one article and 13 in another, so no figure is stated.
stops.campa: The farm above the Grand River has an orchard, a stable, and a carriage house that Alexander converts into a workshop. He calls a spot on the edge of the bluff his dreaming place and goes there to think, lying in the grass with the water below him. In July 1874, on paper and in his head, he works out here the principle he will patent two years later: that a current made to vary in the shape of a sound wave will carry speech. The house is Melville House, and Canada will call it the birthplace of the telephone.
suggested_refs: The Bell Homestead National Historic Site, 94 Tutela Heights Road, Brantford

stops.name: Six Nations of the Grand River, Mohawk in Visible Speech
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The research pool gives only 'the 1870s' and states that the date of the honorary title and the exact village site are unconfirmed. The pin is an Onondaga village location, not a documented one.
stops.campa: Across the river lies the territory of the Six Nations of the Grand River, and Bell walks over to it. Mohawk is a spoken language with no writing of its own; he sits with speakers and sets it down in his father's Visible Speech symbols, one mouth position at a time, until he can read the sounds back aloud to people who have never seen their own language on a page. They make him an honorary chief. He learns the war dance with the title, and performs it afterwards, for the rest of his life, whenever he is pleased with himself.
suggested_refs: The Six Nations of the Grand River reserve, across the river from Tutela Heights
sources: General biographical tradition for the honorary chieftaincy and the war dance

stops.name: Boston School for Deaf Mutes, Pemberton Square
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1871; day defaulted. The Hartford and Northampton demonstrations of 1871-1872 are folded in here rather than pinned separately (American School for the Deaf, Hartford: 41.7658, -72.6890; Clarke School, Northampton: 42.3251, -72.6412).
stops.campa: He travels with his father to Montreal in the spring, watches him demonstrate Visible Speech to a hall, and then goes on alone to Boston to train the teachers of the Boston School for Deaf Mutes in the system, at a salary his father negotiated after declining the post himself. It spreads through New England from there: the American Asylum at Hartford, the Clarke School at Northampton, one demonstration after another before rooms full of instructors. He is twenty-four, Scottish, holds no degree at all, and within a year he is the man American deaf education sends for.
suggested_refs: The Boston School for Deaf Mutes at Pemberton Square, later the Horace Mann School for the Deaf

stops.name: Boston, the School of Vocal Physiology and Mechanics of Speech
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1872. The Boston University professorship is dated 1872 here, following Wikipedia's verbatim wording; the geography lens of the research pool dated it 1873, and that contradiction is recorded in the report and not resolved. Exact street address of the school unconfirmed.
stops.campa: He opens his own School of Vocal Physiology and Mechanics of Speech in Boston with some thirty pupils, and Boston University makes him professor of Vocal Physiology and Elocution in its School of Oratory. He teaches the mechanism of speech by day and works at night on a second problem, the harmonic telegraph: several messages at once along one wire, each carried on a steel reed tuned to its own pitch, each sorted out at the far end by a reed tuned to match. Both problems are one problem. A sound is a shape, and a shape can be sent.
stops.quote: The idea of increasing the carrying power of a telegraph wire in this way took complete possession of my mind, and it was this practical end that I had in view when I commenced my researches in Electric Telephony.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony', London, 31 October 1877, recalling the origin of the harmonic telegraph work
suggested_refs: The Boston University School of Oratory, then in downtown Boston, not the modern Charles River campus

stops.name: Salem, the house of Georgie Sanders
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1873-1875; day defaulted. Exact address within Salem unconfirmed by any source fetched.
stops.campa: He cuts his teaching down to two private pupils. Georgie Sanders is five and deaf from birth; Mabel Hubbard is fifteen, deafened by scarlet fever at five, and reads lips so well that strangers never guess. Bell lodges at the Sanders grandmother's house in Salem and is given the cellar to experiment in. The two fathers, Thomas Sanders the leather merchant and Gardiner Greene Hubbard the lawyer, begin quietly funding the electrical work as an appendix to their children's education. He commutes to Boston, teaches all day, and sleeps very little.
suggested_refs: The Sanders house at Salem, Massachusetts, where the cellar was given over to the apparatus

stops.name: Boston, the reed that was plucked
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: Watson, in one room, plucks a reed on the harmonic telegraph that has stuck fast against its magnet. Bell, in the other room, hears through his own instrument not the single clean pitch he expects but the whole complex twang of the reed, its overtones and its decay, carried down the wire. It means that one membrane vibrating in a magnetic field can transmit any sound whatever, and not merely a tone. He stops working on the telegraph that day. Everything after is the building of a machine to do deliberately what the accident proved possible.
suggested_refs: The harmonic telegraph apparatus of June 1875, first instrument to carry a complex sound

stops.name: Washington, the Patent Office on the fourteenth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested for both filings and for the grant of 7 March. The research pool contains no dedicated source for the Gray priority dispute and flags this as a gap; nothing here adjudicates which document reached the clerk first.
stops.campa: Hubbard's lawyer files Bell's application at the Patent Office on the fourteenth of February. The same morning, in the same building, Elisha Gray files a caveat describing a telephone with a liquid transmitter. Which paper reached the clerk first, and in what order the two were entered in the book, will be litigated for twenty years and argued over for a hundred. On the seventh of March the patent issues to Bell: number 174,465, Improvement in Telegraphy, five claims, of which the fifth is the telephone.
stops.quote: The method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically, as herein described, by causing electrical undulations, similar in form to the vibrations of the air accompanying the said vocal or other sound, substantially as set forth.
stops.quote_source: US Patent No. 174,465, 'Improvement in Telegraphy', claim 5, granted 7 March 1876
suggested_refs: US Patent No. 174,465 and Elisha Gray's caveat of the same day, US Patent Office records
sources: Google Patents, US 174,465 (page carries OCR damage; standard published wording used)

stops.name: Exeter Place, Boston, the first sentence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The address 5 Exeter Place is not named in any article fetched, though the coordinates fall within about 150 m of the historic location. The acid-spill story carried at attested rank by the gathering pass appears in no source and has been dropped.
stops.campa: Three days after the patent issues, the apparatus works. Bell speaks into the transmitter in one room of the boarding house and Watson, at the receiver in the other, hears whole words for the first time and comes running down the passage. Bell writes the sentence into his laboratory notebook that night, with dashes where he paused. Watson's own account, published thirty-seven years later, gives the words differently. The instrument had never carried a sentence before, and the patent had issued three days earlier on the promise that it would.
stops.quote: Mr. Watson—come here—I want to see you.
stops.quote_source: Bell's laboratory notebook, 'Experiments Made by A. Graham Bell, Vol. 1', entry of 10 March 1876, pp. 40-41 (Library of Congress; World Digital Library surrogate WDL11375). Watson's own 1913 memoir gives a different wording: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want you.'
suggested_refs: Bell's laboratory notebook page for 10 March 1876, Alexander Graham Bell Family Papers, Library of Congress
sources: World Digital Library item WDL11375, mirrored on Wikimedia Commons
Thomas A. Watson, 'The Birth and Babyhood of the Telephone' (1913), Gutenberg #54506, for the divergent wording

stops.name: Boston University, the question through the wire
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the date only. Bell recounts the test in his 1877 London lecture without dating it; the month here is assigned to sit between the March success and the June exposition.
stops.campa: He runs the wire from his lecture room at Boston University down into the basement of the adjoining building and sends a student to the far end to listen. The sentence he chooses is the one every early telephone experiment reduces itself to: he asks the machine whether he is understood. The student, in the cellar, understands him. Bell tells the story a year later to the telegraph engineers of London as a matter of laboratory record, in the flat voice of a man reporting a measurement he took and would take again.
stops.quote: One of the telephones was placed in my lecture-room in the Boston University, and the other in the basement of the adjoining building. One of my students repaired to the distant telephone to observe the effects of articulate speech, while I uttered the sentence, 'Do you understand what I say?' into the telephone placed in the lecture-hall.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony', lecture to the Society of Telegraph Engineers, London, 31 October 1877
suggested_refs: Bell's 'Researches in Electric Telephony', Project Gutenberg ebook #55787
sources: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony' (1877), Project Gutenberg #55787

stops.name: Machinery Hall, Philadelphia, the Centennial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exposition and the exhibit. The judging visit of Lord Kelvin and Dom Pedro II, and the exclamation attributed to Dom Pedro, appear in no fetched source: the Centennial Exposition article records only that the telephone stood at opposite ends of Machinery Hall, and places Dom Pedro at the 10 May opening as a state guest. The campa reports the episode as tradition, and no quote field is used.
stops.campa: At the Centennial Exposition the telephone stands at opposite ends of Machinery Hall, two instruments and the length of a building between them. Bell is twenty-nine and unknown outside Boston. The story that survives has Dom Pedro II of Brazil putting the receiver to his ear and crying out that it talks, and William Thomson of Glasgow pronouncing it the most wonderful thing he has seen in America. What the record shows is only that the apparatus was there and that the exposition closed with the instrument famous.
suggested_refs: Machinery Hall, Centennial Exposition, Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, 1876

stops.name: Mount Pleasant, Ontario, the voice from Brantford
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, with the roles corrected: both lenses of the research pool had Bell making the call from Brantford, and one had the line running into the family home. Wikipedia's Bell Homestead article has David Charles Bell speaking from the Brantford telegraph office and Alexander receiving at Mount Pleasant. Coordinates are a village-centre approximation, the weakest pin in this file.
stops.campa: On a summer visit home the family runs the experiment over the Dominion Telegraph line. Bell's uncle, Professor David Charles Bell, speaks from the telegraph office at Brantford; Alexander sits four miles south in a store at Mount Pleasant with the receiver against his ear, and listens. Reception is poor until they connect the line to a battery, and then the voice comes through the wire whole. The inventor of the telephone is on this occasion the man at the other end, which is the position the rest of the world will occupy from now on.
suggested_refs: The Dominion Telegraph line from Brantford to Mount Pleasant, Ontario, 3 August 1876

stops.name: Paris, Ontario, eight miles of telegraph wire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the title of world's first long-distance telephone call is a claim the sources report rather than adjudicate.
stops.campa: A week later they double the distance: Brantford to Paris, eight miles of telegraph wire strung for Morse code and now carrying speech. Canada counts it the first long-distance telephone call in the world. Bell is standing in the town where he lodged with a minister six years earlier, coughing, expecting to die of what had killed both his brothers. The wire runs past the mills on the Grand River, and the apparatus at each end is no different in principle from the thing that failed for two years in a Boston attic.
suggested_refs: The Brantford to Paris telegraph line, Ontario, 10 August 1876

stops.name: Kilby Street, Boston, both directions at once
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The research pool disagrees with itself on the far end: one lens gives the Walworth Manufacturing Company about 2.5 miles off, another frames it as Boston to Cambridge. Not resolved.
stops.campa: On the ninth of October Bell sits at Kilby Street in Boston and Watson at the Walworth works two and a half miles away, and for the first time each hears the other and answers him. Every demonstration until now has been one direction only: a speaker and a listener, a performance with an audience. This is a conversation. Both men keep notes of what was said, and the two sets of notes agree. The telephone stops being an exhibit that evening and becomes a thing two people can use without either of them being its inventor.
stops.quote: I must also express my obligations to my friend and associate, Mr. Thomas A. Watson, of Salem, Massachusetts, who has for two years past given me his personal assistance in carrying on my researches.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony', London, 31 October 1877
suggested_refs: The Walworth Manufacturing Company works, far end of the first two-way call

stops.name: Boston, the Bell Telephone Company
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the founding. The Western Union refusal is dated only 'before 1878' by one article and 'around 1876-78' by another, which also attributes the offer to Hubbard alone rather than to all three partners. Not resolved.
stops.campa: Bell, Hubbard and Sanders form the Bell Telephone Company: no factory, no exchange, no subscribers, and one patent. Before this they had offered the patent outright to Western Union for a hundred thousand dollars and been refused, the telephone being in the judgment of the telegraph monopoly an electrical toy with no commercial future. Within two years the same monopoly is in the telephone business itself and defending a patent suit it will lose, against a company it could have bought entire for the price it declined to pay.
suggested_refs: The founding agreement of the Bell Telephone Company, Boston, 9 July 1877

stops.name: Brattle Street, Cambridge, the wedding and the shares
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates corrected from the gathering pass's 42.3736, -71.1190, which sits near Harvard Yard and not on Brattle Street at all; Nominatim gives 146 Brattle Street as 42.3772249, -71.1314509.
stops.campa: Two days after the company is chartered he marries Mabel Hubbard in her father's house on Brattle Street. She is nineteen and he is thirty; she has been deaf since she was five and his pupil since she was fifteen. For a wedding present he signs over 1,487 of his 1,497 shares in the Bell Telephone Company, keeping ten. The stock is worth almost nothing that week. Mabel will hold it for thirty years and then spend a piece of it on aeroplanes. They sail for Europe on a honeymoon that runs more than a year.
suggested_refs: The Hubbard estate on Brattle Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts

stops.name: London, the Society of Telegraph Engineers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, from Bell's own published lecture text.
stops.campa: He reads a paper to the Society of Telegraph Engineers in London: the whole history of the work laid out in order, the harmonic telegraph, the stuck reed, the membrane, the shape of the current. He names Watson by name and thanks him for two years of personal assistance. He reports that conversation has already been carried through sixty miles of submarine cable, from Dartmouth to the island of Guernsey. The speaking telephone is nineteen months old, and its inventor is standing in the capital of the country he left as a consumptive schoolmaster, explaining it to engineers.
stops.quote: It is to-night my pleasure, as well as duty, to give you some account of the telephonic researches in which I have been so long engaged.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony', Society of Telegraph Engineers, London, 31 October 1877, opening line
suggested_refs: 'Researches in Electric Telephony', Bell's own published lecture, Project Gutenberg ebook #55787
sources: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Researches in Electric Telephony' (1877), Project Gutenberg #55787

stops.name: Osborne House, the demonstration to the Queen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates corrected from the gathering pass's 50.7460, -1.2793, about 850 m off and outside the house; Wikipedia gives 50.75056, -1.26972. The Queen's words are reported as 'quite extraordinary' in Wikipedia and as 'most extraordinary' in the gathering pass, so no quote field is used.
stops.campa: He is summoned to Osborne House on the Isle of Wight to show the instrument to Queen Victoria, and lines are run out from the house to Cowes, to Southampton, and to London. She finds the sound rather faint and the thing itself quite extraordinary, and asks whether an apparatus can be got for her. Nineteen months earlier the same invention stood on a table in Machinery Hall with almost nobody certain what it was for. The Queen of the United Kingdom has now asked to buy one.
suggested_refs: Osborne House, East Cowes, Isle of Wight, and Queen Victoria's journal entry for 14 January 1878

stops.name: Franklin School, Washington, the beam of light
stops.date_confidence: disputed, three ways, across Wikipedia itself: the Bell biography says 21 June 1880, the Photophone article says 3 June 1880, and the Volta Laboratory article says 1 April 1880 while noting a plaque giving 3 June. The June date is used here. Coordinates corrected from 38.9008, -77.0272 to the Franklin School article's 38.90222, -77.02972.
stops.campa: From the roof of the Franklin School at Thirteenth and K, Charles Sumner Tainter aims a beam of sunlight at a mirror made to vibrate with his voice, and seven hundred feet away, at the laboratory window on L Street, Bell hears him speak. There is no wire anywhere in the arrangement. The photophone modulates light itself, and Bell holds it to be the greatest invention he ever made, greater than the telephone. Voice carried by radio is nineteen years off. Nothing practical comes of the photophone in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The Franklin School at 13th and K Streets NW, Washington, and the photophone apparatus of 1880

stops.name: Volta Laboratory, Connecticut Avenue, Washington
stops.date_confidence: attested for the laboratory's existence 1880-1886, but a single pin cannot represent it: the laboratory sat first at 1325 L Street NW, then at 1221 Connecticut Avenue NW, then at 2020 F Street NW after January 1886. Coordinates are Nominatim's for the Connecticut Avenue address, corrected from the gathering pass's 38.9089, -77.0407.
stops.campa: France awards him the Volta Prize, fifty thousand francs, for the telephone, and he spends it on a laboratory named for Volta: himself, Tainter, and his cousin Chichester Bell, working on the recording of sound. What comes out of it is the graphophone, wax instead of Edison's tinfoil, and it earns more money than anything Bell touches after the telephone itself. The name carries forward: at Como in 1927, at the centenary of the same Alessandro Volta, Enrico Fermi and Paul Dirac will sit among the physicists arguing out the new mechanics.
suggested_refs: The Volta Laboratory at 1221 Connecticut Avenue NW, and the graphophone patents of 1886
sources: Atlas crossing: fermi.journey.json and dirac.journey.json, Volta congress at Como

stops.name: Scott Circle, Washington, the Brodhead mansion
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1882-1889 as the family's Washington residence, and for the naturalisation in 1882; day defaulted. The causes of the two infants' deaths are not given in any source fetched and are not stated.
stops.campa: The family takes the Brodhead mansion near Scott Circle, and Bell becomes an American citizen, born a British subject, his fortune made between Canada and the United States. Two sons are born in this house and neither lives: Edward in 1881, Robert in 1883, both dying in infancy. The daughters, Elsie and Daisy, survive them. Bell turns from the sons he could not keep to the question of what is passed down and what is not, and writes the worst thing he ever wrote.
suggested_refs: The Brodhead-Bell mansion at Scott Circle, Washington, D.C.

stops.name: Washington, the memoir on a deaf variety of the human race
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; day defaulted. The much-quoted sentence about the impropriety of intermarriage is not Bell's own: he is quoting the Rev. W. W. Turner's 1868 paper, and it is therefore not used as a quote here.
stops.campa: He reads to the National Academy of Sciences a memoir arguing that deaf people marrying deaf people, generation upon generation, in a country that gathers them into residential schools and lets them build a language of their own, will produce in time a deaf variety of the human race. He proposes no law and no prohibition. He proposes day schools, spoken language, and the ending of sign. Deaf America will spend the next hundred years undoing what the paper set moving, and will name him in it as the adversary.
stops.quote: If the laws of heredity that are known to hold in the case of animals also apply to man, the intermarriage of congenital deaf-mutes through a number of successive generations should result in the formation of a deaf variety of the human race.
stops.quote_source: Alexander Graham Bell, 'Memoir Upon the Formation of a Deaf Variety of the Human Race', National Academy of Sciences, 1883
suggested_refs: 'Memoir Upon the Formation of a Deaf Variety of the Human Race' (1883), Internet Archive gu_memoirformati00bell

stops.name: Washington, the deafblind child
stops.date_confidence: traditional for the year: Wikipedia gives no more precise date than about 1886, when Keller was six. The Perkins referral and Anne Sullivan's appointment are general biographical consensus, not present in this research pool.
stops.campa: A father brings him a six-year-old girl from Alabama who has been deaf and blind since infancy and has no language of any kind. Bell sits her on his knee, lets her feel his watch tick, and understands her immediately. He sends the family on to the Perkins Institution, which sends them Anne Sullivan. Helen Keller will dedicate her autobiography to him and say that he gave his life to breaching the inhuman silence which separates and estranges. In 1952 she stands in Paris to speak at the transfer of Louis Braille's ashes to the Panthéon.
suggested_refs: Helen Keller's dedication in 'The Story of My Life' (1903)
sources: Atlas crossing: braille.journey.json, stop 'The Panthéon, the ashes borne among the great of France'

stops.name: Kendall Green, the address on marriage to the deaf
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the speech to the Literary Society of Kendall Green, and to 1898 for the Volta Bureau printing. The pamphlet was verified this pass by its Internet Archive bibliographic record only and was not read in full; the quoted sentences come from the Bell Legacy Foundation, an interested party, and are not checked against the pamphlet text. Historians disagree on what Bell sought: Greenwald and Van Cleve (2015) hold that he resisted restricting deaf people's marriage rights, while the Princeton blurb for Greenwald's own 2024 talk says he sought to dissuade deaf people from marrying each other. Not resolved.
stops.campa: He stands before the Literary Society at Kendall Green, in the deaf college in northeast Washington, eight years after the memoir, and tells the students to their faces that he has never tried to stop them marrying and does not intend to. The Volta Bureau prints the address in 1898 as Marriage: An Address to the Deaf, with an essay on consanguineous marriages bound in behind it. The man who warned the National Academy that deaf intermarriage would breed a deaf variety of the human race tells a hall of deaf students they can marry whom they choose. Both texts carry his name.
stops.quote: You can marry whom you choose, and I hope you will be happy.
stops.quote_source: Bell, address to the Literary Society of Kendall Green, Washington, 6 March 1891, as quoted by the Alexander & Mabel Bell Legacy Foundation, an interested party; the Volta Bureau pamphlet of 1898 that reprints the address was not read in full for this pass
suggested_refs: 'Marriage: An Address to the Deaf', Volta Bureau, Washington, 1898, Internet Archive gu_marriageaddre00bell
sources: Alexander & Mabel Bell Legacy Foundation, belllegacy.org, for the quoted sentences
Brian H. Greenwald and John Vickrey Van Cleve, 'A Deaf Variety of the Human Race', Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era 14:1 (2015), 28-48, abstract only

stops.name: Volta Bureau, Georgetown, the endowment for the deaf
stops.date_confidence: attested: bureau founded 1887, building constructed 1893, National Historic Landmark 28 November 1972. The research pool gives two street numbers for the same corner, 1537 35th Street NW and 3417 Volta Place NW, so neither is stated here.
stops.campa: He endows the Volta Bureau in Georgetown out of his own prize money, for the increase and diffusion of knowledge relating to the deaf, and in 1893 Helen Keller, thirteen years old, turns the first spadeful of earth for its building. The neoclassical block still stands and still houses the association that carries his name. In 1898 he takes the presidency of the National Geographic Society, turns its magazine toward photographs, and writes for it under the byline H. A. Largelamb, which is his own name rearranged.
suggested_refs: The Volta Bureau building, Georgetown, by Peabody and Stearns, a National Historic Landmark

stops.name: Baddeck, the mountain that looked like home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the first visit; month inferred from the summer escape the sources describe.
stops.campa: Escaping the Washington heat, the Bells cross to Cape Breton Island and come up the Bras d'Or lakes by steamer to the village of Baddeck. The hills across the water are bare and green and rise straight out of salt water, and they look like Scotland. Bell is thirty-eight and has not lived in Scotland since he was twenty-three. He begins buying land on the headland opposite the village the following year, and for the last thirty years of his life this is where the work gets done.
suggested_refs: Baddeck village and the Bras d'Or lakes, Cape Breton Island

stops.name: Beinn Bhreagh, the Lodge and the great house
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Lodge 1888, Beinn Bhreagh Hall 1893, corrected from the gathering pass's 'by 1889'. Coordinates corrected from 46.0917, -60.7233 to Wikipedia's 46.094611, -60.715972, a shift of about 650 m.
stops.campa: He names the headland Beinn Bhreagh, beautiful mountain, in the Gaelic of a country he left as a boy; the Mi'kmaq have called it Megwatpatek, red head, for very much longer. The Lodge goes up in 1888 and the great house in 1893, and around them a boatyard, laboratories, workshops, and a shed for kites. He employs a good part of the neighbourhood. Washington becomes the place the family winters and Cape Breton the place where anything gets built, which is the arrangement for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Beinn Bhreagh Hall and the Lodge, Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia

stops.name: Beinn Bhreagh, the tetrahedral cell
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The gathering pass dated man-lifting tetrahedral kites to 1898; Wikipedia runs the kite work 1895-1910 with the tetrahedral cell developed c. 1899-1903, and man-lifting achieved only in December 1907.
stops.campa: He is flying kites off the headland, and the obstacle is arithmetic: a kite large enough to lift a man is too heavy to fly. The answer he finds is a shape. Four triangles close into a cell that is rigid in every direction and almost entirely air, and the cell can be repeated to any size at all without losing its ratio of strength to weight. He builds them by the thousand out of spruce sticks and red silk. Buckminster Fuller will reach the century's other answer to the same question, and it is the same triangle.
suggested_refs: The tetrahedral kites of Beinn Bhreagh, 1899-1910, and the kite house on the estate
sources: Atlas crossing: buckminster_fuller.journey.json, no meeting attested

stops.name: Baddeck, the Aerial Experiment Association
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the founding and for the four members. Mabel Bell's financing is attested; the twenty thousand dollar figure and her sale of property to raise it are general biographical consensus rather than pool sources.
stops.campa: Mabel puts money of her own into an association of five: her husband, aged sixty, and four young men. Glenn Curtiss builds the fastest engines in America at Hammondsport. Casey Baldwin and Douglas McCurdy are Toronto engineering graduates who came for a summer. Thomas Selfridge is a lieutenant of the United States Army. The purpose is written down in a single line, to get a man into the air by their own means, and the association gives itself eighteen months and a table in the Bells' house to do it.
suggested_refs: The founding agreement of the Aerial Experiment Association, Baddeck, 30 September 1907

stops.name: Bras d'Or Lake, the Cygnet lifts a man
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, corrected out of the gathering pass, which had folded man-lifting into an 1898 kite entry. Selfridge's death at Fort Myer nine months later is general knowledge and is not in this research pool.
stops.campa: The Cygnet is thousands of tetrahedral cells assembled into one hollow wing, and it is towed off Baddeck behind a steamer with Thomas Selfridge lying inside it. It rises a hundred and sixty-eight feet above the water, carrying him, and comes down again onto the lake. He is twenty-six. Nine months later Selfridge is killed at Fort Myer as a passenger in Orville Wright's machine, the first human being to die in a powered aeroplane, and the association goes on with four.
suggested_refs: The Cygnet man-lifting kite, towed off Baddeck, 6 December 1907

stops.name: Hammondsport, the Red Wing and the June Bug
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the Red Wing; the June Bug's kilometre flight and Scientific American Trophy are attested to 1908 without a day in this pool.
stops.campa: The association winters at Curtiss's motorcycle works at Hammondsport on Keuka Lake, where the engines are. On the twelfth of March the Red Wing rises off the lake ice with Casey Baldwin at the controls, and a Canadian and British subject flies a powered aeroplane for the first time. In July the June Bug carries Curtiss a full kilometre in front of official observers and takes the Scientific American Trophy, the first publicly witnessed flight of that distance anywhere in North America.
suggested_refs: The Curtiss works at Hammondsport, Keuka Lake, New York, winter base of the association

stops.name: Bras d'Or ice, the Silver Dart
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the flight and to 31 March 1909 for the dissolution. That the flight was also a first for the British Empire is a common claim not present in the sources fetched.
stops.campa: On the ice of Bras d'Or Lake, with the village of Baddeck standing along the shore to watch, Douglas McCurdy flies the Silver Dart off the frozen surface: the first controlled powered flight in Canada. Bell watches from the ice. Five weeks later the Aerial Experiment Association dissolves itself, having done precisely what it was formed to do and having said in advance that it would stop when it did. The four young men go out into an aircraft industry that does not exist yet and will need all of them.
suggested_refs: The Silver Dart and the ice of Bras d'Or Lake, 23 February 1909

stops.name: Paris, the Langley Medal into Eiffel's hands
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year from the atlas's own Eiffel file; day and month defaulted, and the venue of the Smithsonian ceremony is not located. Eiffel's drop experiments from his tower are general knowledge, not in this research pool.
stops.campa: The Smithsonian sends him to Paris to put the Samuel P. Langley Medal for Aerodromics into the hands of Gustave Eiffel, who is eighty and has spent a decade dropping weighted shapes down a cable from his own tower to measure the resistance of the air. Bell tells him that his writings on the subject are already classical. Two old men stand in one room, each of them a builder of impossible structures out of one small triangle repeated: Bell's kites of spruce stick and red silk, Eiffel's riveted iron over the Champ de Mars.
suggested_refs: The Samuel P. Langley Medal for Aerodromics, Smithsonian Institution, awarded to Eiffel in 1913
sources: Atlas crossing: gustave_eiffel.journey.json, stop 'Paris, the Langley Medal'

stops.name: 15 Dey Street, New York, the continent crossed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The Panama-Pacific Exposition framing carried by the gathering pass is dropped: the exposition opened 20 February 1915, nearly a month after the call. Watson's reported reply is tradition, not in the pool.
stops.campa: At the AT&T building on Dey Street, Bell lifts a telephone and speaks to Thomas Watson at 333 Grant Avenue in San Francisco, some three thousand four hundred miles off, and repeats the sentence from the Boston boarding house. Watson answers that it would take him a week to come now. Bell is sixty-seven. The company carrying the call will one day fund a laboratory bearing his name on West Street, where Claude Shannon works out what information is, and this wire in his hand is the first length of that line.
suggested_refs: The AT&T headquarters at 15 Dey Street, New York, and 333 Grant Avenue, San Francisco
sources: Atlas crossing: claude_shannon.journey.json, Bell Telephone Laboratories, 463 West Street

stops.name: Cold Spring Harbor, the chair at the Eugenics Record Office
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the board meeting, from the photograph published in Eugenical News vol. 14 no. 8 and reproduced by the Eugenics Archive. The chairmanship itself is dated from 1912 by some sources and from 1913 by others, and the board is called 'scientific advisers' in some and 'scientific directors' in others; neither contradiction is resolved here. No ERO minutes or annual reports were read, so what Bell said or voted in that chair is unknown to this file. Nothing was found in this pass on the immigration-restriction advocacy often attributed to him, and none is asserted.
stops.campa: At Cold Spring Harbor, in the Eugenics Record Office that Charles Davenport founded in 1910 on Harriman, Rockefeller and Carnegie money, Bell sits at the head of the Board of Scientific Directors. Eugenical News prints the photograph of the board meeting of the tenth of April 1915: the economist Irving Fisher, the geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan, and the inventor of the telephone, sixty-eight years old, captioned as chairman. The office gathers family pedigrees by the tens of thousands and advises on fitness for marriage. He holds the chair until 1918.
suggested_refs: The Eugenics Record Office board photograph of 10 April 1915, Eugenical News vol. 14 no. 8, Cold Spring Harbor, New York
sources: Eugenics Archive, eugenicsarchive.org, theme page on the Eugenics Record Office, citing Eugenical News vol. 14 no. 8
DNA Learning Center, Cold Spring Harbor, item 10950, Eugenics Record Office organisational description
DNA Learning Center, items 10406 to 10408, American Breeders Association descriptions, for Bell's chairmanship of the Committee on Heredity of Deaf-mutism under the ABA Eugenics Section

stops.name: Brantford, the memorial unveiled
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: Brantford unveils a monument to the telephone in a park at the end of West Street: Walter Seymour Allward's bronze and granite, allegorical figures of Knowledge, Joy and Sorrow, and a man lying prone, transmitting sound through space. The town began raising money for it in 1906 and raised more than sixty-five thousand dollars; the war delayed the work five years past its intended date. The Duke of Devonshire pulls the cord. Bell is seventy and alive, and the country he arrived in as a dying schoolteacher has built his monument early.
suggested_refs: The Bell Telephone Memorial by Walter Seymour Allward, Bell Memorial Park, Brantford

stops.name: Bras d'Or Lake, the HD-4 at seventy-one miles an hour
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, speed and place. The duration of the record is corrected: the gathering pass said about two decades, and Wikipedia's HD-4 article says almost a year, before Gar Wood took it in Miss America.
stops.campa: Bell is seventy-two and Casey Baldwin is thirty-seven, and the hydrofoil they have built at the Beinn Bhreagh boatyard lifts its hull clear of the water on ladders of submerged wings and runs at seventy-one miles an hour. It is the fastest boat in the world. The record stands about a year before Gar Wood takes it in Miss America. The last thing invented by the man who invented the telephone is a boat that flies, tried out on the lake below his own window in the last summers he has.
suggested_refs: The HD-4 hydrofoil, preserved at the Alexander Graham Bell National Historic Site, Baddeck

stops.name: Beinn Bhreagh, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, aged 75, of complications from diabetes. Coordinates corrected from the afterlife lens's 46.1, -60.75, which is Baddeck village across the bay. The signed exchange at the bedside is reported widely and is not independently verified in this pool.
stops.campa: He dies at Beinn Bhreagh in the small hours, seventy-five years old, of complications of diabetes, with Mabel beside him. She signs to him not to leave her. He is past speech by then and answers her in the language of his pupils and his mother and his wife, shaping the sign for no with his fingers. It is his last communication. Below the house the boatyard and the kite shed and the laboratory are all still working, and the man who spent his life teaching the deaf to speak goes out of the world in sign.
suggested_refs: Beinn Bhreagh Hall, Cape Breton Island, where Bell died on 2 August 1922

stops.name: Beinn Bhreagh summit, the burial
stops.date_confidence: burial location attested by Wikipedia and promoted from the gathering pass's reconstruction tag; the day is the funeral date given by the afterlife lens. The silencing of the telephone system is reported by Biography.com with sources differing on whether it fell at the funeral or at the moment of burial, and no instrument count is asserted.
stops.campa: They carry him to the top of the mountain he named in Gaelic and bury him there, above the lake where the Silver Dart flew and the HD-4 ran, in a grave cut into the rock of his own headland. Mabel is buried beside him within the year. It is said that every telephone on the North American continent fell silent for one full minute while he was lowered in, every exchange in two countries stopped at the same moment. The accounts differ on whether the silence fell at the funeral or at the grave.
suggested_refs: The grave atop Beinn Bhreagh mountain, on the private estate, overlooking Bras d'Or Lake
sources: Biography.com, 'Alexander Graham Bell', for the minute of silence

stops.name: The Smithsonian, the voice on the wax disc
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day of announcement, corrected from the gathering pass's 6 May 2013. Smithsonian Magazine returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the source used is Wikipedia's Volta Laboratory article rather than the Smithsonian's own text.
stops.campa: For a hundred and thirty years the Smithsonian holds discs of wax on cardboard out of the Volta Laboratory that no stylus can safely be set down on. In 2013 the museum announces that an optical process, which photographs a groove and computes the sound from the picture without touching anything, has got the audio off them. On a disc dated the fifteenth of April 1885, a man states his name for the record. It is the only known recording of the voice, and the voice is identifying itself so that it can be identified later.
stops.quote: Hear my voice. ... Alexander. . Graham. . Bell.
stops.quote_source: Wax-on-cardboard disc dated 15 April 1885, Volta Laboratory, recovered by the Smithsonian using the IRENE optical technique and announced 23 April 2013
suggested_refs: The Volta Laboratory disc collection at the Smithsonian, and the IRENE optical recovery process developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
